newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Ex-top judge says Albania becoming police state.
newsitem.headline: Ex-top judge says Albania becoming police state.

text.p: Albania's former top judge has accused President Sali Berisha and his right-wing government of receiving money from pyramid schemes to fund election campaigns and of turning the country into a police state.

Zef Brozi, who now lives in the United States, was president of the supreme court until he was sacked by Berisha in September 1995. He called for the government's resignation and a fresh general election by March.
"The current situation in Albania is very tense and dangerous," Brozi said in a faxed statement received by Reuters on Saturday. "Albania is becoming a military and police compound."
"President Berisha and his government are directly responsible for its failed economic policy and the tragedy caused by the collapse of pyramid schemes," he added.

Demonstrations and violent clashes have spread across the Balkan state in the past three weeks after thousands of people took to the streets to protest against collapsing pyramid schemes in which they had invested huge sums of money.
Berisha took on special powers last Sunday to use the army to restore order. Police and security forces were reported to have deployed in trouble spots to clamp down on dissent.
Some 149 people were detained this week and charged with instigating violence in the rash of protests last weekend. They could face at least 15 years' jail if convicted.
Brozi said he supported the demonstrations as the fundamental right of every Albanian to press for change.

He sided with opposition parties in accusing Berisha and his ruling Democratic Party of encouraging pyramid schemes for political ends, in particular during a disputed general election last May and local polls in October.
"The Democratic Party received financial support from the pyramid schemes and threatened people with the loss of their money if they voted for opposition parties," he said.
Berisha has repeatedly denied his party received any money from the investment schemes, but said the main opposition Socialist Party had done so.
"The government which stole the people's votes in May and October is now stealing the people's money," Brozi charged.

Brozi fell out with Berisha's government after speaking out against the jailing of Socialist Party leader Fatos Nano. He was sacked in 1995 after telling a preliminary appeals hearing that he believed Nano, Berisha's main political rival, was innocent and should be freed.
Nano was jailed in 1994 on charges relating to an Italian aid scandal during his short stint as prime minister in Albania's reformist communist administration in 1991.
Defence lawyers have accused the government of holding Nano as a political prisoner and manipulating the judicial system to keep him away from the political scene.
International human rights groups, including Amnesty International, and some Western governments have urged Berisha to release Nano but their appeals have been ignored.
Nano, 43, was sentenced to 12 years in jail. He has had his term cut and now has about 18 months left to serve.
Brozi said he had also appealed to U.S. and European governments, the Council of Europe and other international institutions to stop supporting Berisha and his government.
